Earlier this year, after introducing parental managed accounts for children under 13, WhatsApp is today expanding its parental supervision features to teen accounts, adding group activity notifications and additional restrictions on Meta AI. Here are the details.

WhatsApp Expands Parental Supervision Options

Earlier this year, WhatsApp announced a series of new features giving parents greater control over accounts belonging to children under 13.

These include letting parents decide who can contact the account, which groups they can join, reviewing message requests from unknown contacts, and managing privacy settings — with all changes protected by a PIN set by the parent.

A few weeks later, WhatsApp further expanded the feature on iOS by adding a dedicated "Parental Supervision" section in the Settings app, making it easier for parents to find and configure the accounts they manage.

WhatsApp is once again expanding these supervision features today — this time bringing parental controls to teen users rather than only children under 13 — while offering parents greater transparency over group activity, and more say over how their children interact with channels, status updates, and, perhaps more importantly, Meta AI.

With this update, parents can receive notifications when their children join or leave a group, as well as when the membership of a group they are already in "significantly increases." Parents can also choose how their children use channels, see whose status updates they are able to view, and determine who can see their children's own status updates.

As for Meta AI, parents can now choose between the standard experience designed for users aged 13 and above, and a stricter "limited content" option, depending on what they consider appropriate for their children.

WhatsApp says the limited setting will further restrict the topics that teens can discuss with Meta AI. When enabled, Meta AI features that rely on Private Processing will also become unavailable.

WhatsApp also reiterated that these parental supervision features will not allow parents to read their children's actual messages or calls, as that content remains protected by end-to-end encryption.
